deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Riemann's draft text for the public disputation that accompanied his doctoral promotion at Göttingen (December 1851). It is a cleaner version of the draft on the previous folio. There are no computations on the page. It is a methodological and polemical statement about the definition of 'function of a complex variable'.

(1) Purpose. The dissertation ('Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Größe') was not written polemically. Because it supplies the material for the disputation, Riemann will single out points where 'men of recognized reputation' hold an opposing conviction.

(2) First point: the definition of 'function of a variable complex quantity'. Riemann's definition (as in Diss. §1): w is a function of z = x+iy if w varies with z so that the value of dw/dz is independent of the value of dz. In modern terms, the limit of Δw/Δz exists and does not depend on the direction of Δz. With w = u+iv and differentiable u, v, this is equivalent (my addition) to ∂w/∂x = -i ∂w/∂y, i.e. u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x (Cauchy–Riemann). It is also equivalent to ∂w/∂z̄ = 0.

(3) Opposing views, as far as Riemann knows them.
(a) First view. The property 'dw/dz independent of dz' is ascribed to functions of z but is not taken as the definition. Instead it is derived from an allegedly previously proved theorem: d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b).
(b) Second view, attributed to Cauchy. Any complex quantity w varying with z = x+iy in an arbitrary (in general definite) way is called a function of x+iy. Riemann cites Cauchy's statement at the Paris Academy session of 31 March 1851, made in a report on Puiseux's memoir on algebraic functions, and developed in several later notes.

(4) Comparison.
- View (a) ascribes Riemann's defining property to functions but does not treat it as definitional.
- View (b) does not ascribe the property at all.

(5) Beginning of the critique of (a). For real a, b and real f, the theorem d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b) follows immediately from the concept of derivative. The continuation on the next folio explains why: the derivative is the limit of the ratio of the increment of f to the increment of the argument a+b. It is irrelevant whether that increment is credited to a or to b.

The implied point, which is mine as stated here but evidently where the argument is going: the theorem does not transfer automatically to complex increments. Take a = x and b = iy. Then 'derivative w.r.t. x equals derivative w.r.t. iy' means ∂f/∂x = (1/i)∂f/∂y. That is exactly the Cauchy–Riemann condition, a genuine restriction on f. Hence the theorem cannot be 'proved' for an arbitrary complex-valued dependence on (x, y). It holds only if one already assumes what Riemann takes as the definition.
errors: No mathematical errors on the page; the argument is correct as far as it goes.

The claim that d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b) follows immediately holds for real increments. The page has not yet spelled out the failure for complex increments; that critique is implicit and continues beyond this folio.

results.what: Definition of a function of a complex variable as a dependence w(z) whose derivative dw/dz is independent of dz (direction-independent complex differentiability)
results.modern_name: Holomorphic (complex-differentiable) function; Cauchy–Riemann equations as definition
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Inaugural dissertation 1851 (equations earlier in d'Alembert, Euler, Cauchy)

results.what: Critique of deriving complex differentiability from the theorem d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b): valid for real arguments, but for b = iy it amounts to the Cauchy–Riemann condition itself
results.modern_name: Distinction between real-differentiable functions of (x,y) and holomorphic functions

results.what: Historical report: Cauchy's statement of 31 March 1851 (report on Puiseux) treating any dependence on x+iy as a 'function', later developed in further notes

deep.surprise_reason: This is Riemann's disputation draft defending the well-known definition from his 1851 dissertation. The explicit polemic against Cauchy's March 1851 position is a nice historical detail of his self-positioning. It is mathematically routine, and the disputation materials are known to Riemann scholars (e.g. Laugwitz).

checkable.asserts: z^2 satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann condition ∂f/∂x = -i ∂f/∂y, so dw/dz is independent of dz
For w = conj(z), ∂f/∂x + i∂f/∂y = 2 ≠ 0, so dw/dz depends on dz; under Cauchy's broad view this would still count as a 'function'
In the real case d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b) holds identically
The difference quotient of conj(z) along direction e^{it} equals e^{-2it}, which depends on the direction of dz

transcription_corrections: Folio number '100' at top right and archival note 'Riemann 13' at top left; neither is in the transcription.
In the Cauchy sentence, the words read as 'zuerst [?] und am meisten' are uncertain in the image; possibly 'nebst andern am meisten'. This should remain flagged as uncertain.

Otherwise the transcription matches the image well: '(allgemein zu reden auf bestimmte Art) aber auf ganz beliebige Art', the deletion '[-Ansicht-] Überzeugung', and the deletion '[-Beg-] Begriffs' are all confirmed.
